common_name: Pollypetite Rose of Sharon (True-Dwarf Lavender-Purple Compact Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this true-dwarf selection needs little pruning to hold its naturally rounded shape.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pollypetite stays naturally compact and rounded, so unlike full-size rose of sharon it rarely needs hard pruning to stay in scale with small beds, foundations, or large containers. It opens large, ruffled, solid lavender-purple flowers with no contrasting central eye against dark green foliage, blooming continuously from summer into fall. The plant sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling problem common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon types, and tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established. Water regularly the first season; thereafter it is tolerant of normal garden moisture and needs only an occasional light shaping cut.

common_name: Collie Mullens Rose of Sharon (Historic Semi-Double Fuchsia-Pink Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this older, taller cultivar benefits from underplanting to hide its bare lower stems.

directions: Plant in rich, fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. A nineteenth-century heirloom still in trade today, Collie Mullens carries crepe-textured, semi-double to double fuchsia-pink flowers with a deep burgundy-red throat along upright, somewhat open branches from midsummer into early fall. It grows taller and leggier than most modern compact rose of sharon selections, often clearing several feet of bare stem at the base, so it looks best underplanted with lower shrubs or perennials or used as a loose screen rather than a tidy specimen. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established; prune selectively in late winter to control height and remove crowded interior growth.

common_name: Mahogany Splendor Hibiscus (Deeply Cut Burgundy Maple-Leaf Foliage Hibiscus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or set out rooted cuttings and nursery starts after frost danger passes, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; foliage color deepens with more direct sun.

directions: Grown almost entirely for its foliage, Mahogany Splendor produces deeply lobed, serrated, maple-shaped leaves in a rich burgundy-maroon that looks strikingly like a Japanese maple on a fast-growing tropical shrub. Its small pale pink to reddish flowers appear through summer but are mostly hidden among the dark leaves, so the real show is the season-long color and texture contrast it adds to beds and mixed containers. Plant in full sun for the deepest leaf color and heat tolerance; it is drought-tolerant once established but performs best with regular water. It grows as a root-hardy perennial in the warmest part of zone 9 and in zones 10-11, and as a fast warm-season annual elsewhere, reaching full size in a single growing season.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Henderson County Master Gardeners)

common_name: Red Shield Hibiscus (Compact Burgundy Maple-Leaf Tropical Foliage Shrub)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after frost danger passes, in evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Red Shield carries iridescent maroon, three- to five-lobed, maple-shaped foliage on a fast-growing, vigorous tropical shrub, with small two-inch burgundy flowers that tend to disappear visually against the dark leaves. It tolerates more shade than many foliage tropicals, holding reasonable color from full sun into fairly shaded spots, though leaf color is richest with several hours of direct sun. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season and pinch young plants to encourage a fuller, bushier shape rather than a single leggy stem. It is killed back by temperatures in the upper 30s, so treat it as a warm-season annual or container plant outside the mild winters of zone 9b-11, overwintering cuttings indoors if desired.

common_name: Seminole Pink Hibiscus (Heirloom Soft Pink Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: An old South Florida heirloom believed to date to a Miami-Dade nursery of the 1960s, Seminole Pink bears large, single, soft pastel-pink flowers with a deeper pink center, four to six inches across, on a dense, self-branching, upright shrub. It blooms prolifically through the warm season with little fuss, which has kept it in Florida landscapes and at historic sites for decades even as newer, flashier tropical hibiscus cultivars have come and gone. Grow it in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil and regular feeding through the growing season; prune after flushes of bloom to maintain a dense habit. Protect from frost or grow in a container to overwinter indoors outside the warmest zones.

common_name: Suva Queen Hibiscus (Double Clear Pink Fijian Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Originating in Fiji, Suva Queen is a vigorous, upright tropical hibiscus grown for its fully double, clear pink flowers, produced heavily from late spring through summer on a warm, sunny, sheltered plant. Its strong, somewhat sprawling growth benefits from occasional pruning after the main flush of bloom to keep the shrub full and well-shaped rather than open and leggy. Give it full sun, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and regular warm-season feeding for the best flower production. In cooler climates it grows well in a large container that can be moved under cover when temperatures drop below about 40°F.
sources: Australian and New Zealand specialty nursery trade listings
